history.title: Read Around the Word

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

You already do this. When you hit a word you do not know, you keep reading and you often work it out. This week you learn the moves you were already making, so you can use them on purpose.

1. Read **The Words Around the Word**.
2. Learn the words in **Clue Words**, then win the **Crossword**.
3. Keep the **Four Kinds of Clue** chart where you can see it.
4. Sort the cards in **Which Clue Is It?**
5. Say the **Word Detective Frames** out loud with a partner.
6. Take **Word Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Four Clues**.
8. Read **Word Questions Kids Ask** — one answer says when to give up and look it up.
9. Finish with **Design: A Clue Hunt for a Reading Buddy**.

Your job this week: catch yourself working out one real word while reading, and tell somebody how you did it. 🔍

history.title: The Words Around the Word
history.data:
## The Words Around the Word

Read this: *The path was so narrow that we had to walk single file.*

Suppose you did not know **narrow**. You would still have a good guess. If people have to walk one behind the other, the path must be thin. You did not look anything up. The sentence told you.

That is what a **context** **clue** is. The words around a word hint at what it means. You have been doing it since you were small.

There are four kinds worth knowing by name.

Sometimes the writer just tells you. *A glacier, a huge slow-moving river of ice, carved this valley.* That is a **definition** clue, and it is the easiest one.

Sometimes you get cases instead. *She packed produce: apples, carrots, and lettuce.* Nobody defined produce, but the **example** clue shows you it means fruits and vegetables.

Sometimes a nearby word means almost the same thing. *He was furious. I had never seen him so angry.* Angry is a **synonym**, and it hands you the meaning.

Sometimes the sentence swings the other way. *The room was not tidy; it was a shambles.* The little word not tells you a shambles is the opposite of tidy. That is an **antonym** clue.

Watch for **signal** words. Or, that is, and such as often bring a definition or an example. But, however and instead often bring an opposite.

The word itself can help too. A **prefix** is a word part on the front. Un- means not, so unhappy is not happy. A **suffix** is a word part on the end. -ful means full of, so joyful is full of joy. Underneath is the **root**, the main part carrying the meaning.

Now the honest part. Sometimes there is no clue at all. The sentence gives you nothing, and guessing harder will not help. That is the moment to ask someone or use a dictionary. Knowing when to stop guessing is a reading skill too.

history.title: Clue Words

data.def: The words and sentences around a word that hint at what it means.
A hint that helps you work something out.
A sentence that tells you straight out what a word means.
A case given to show what a word covers.
A word that means nearly the same as another word.
A word that means the opposite of another word.
A word part added to the front that changes the meaning.
A word part added to the end that changes the meaning.
The main part of a word, the part that carries its meaning.
A small word like or, but, or such as that tells you a hint is coming.

data.title: Remember the Four Clues
data.instructions: Two cards hold the moves. Look at the example, make one your own, then say how it helps you.
data.sourceExcerpt: Sometimes the writer just tells you. Sometimes you get cases instead. Sometimes a nearby word means almost the same thing. Sometimes the sentence swings the other way.

cards.target: The four kinds of context clue a sentence can give you
essentialFacts: A definition clue tells you the meaning straight out.
An example clue shows you cases instead.
A synonym clue puts a word nearby that means nearly the same.
An antonym clue puts a word nearby that means the opposite.
cards.aiExample: D-E-S-A: Dogs Eat Some Apples. Definition, Example, Synonym, Antonym. Silly on purpose, because silly sticks.
cards.mapping: Each first letter is one kind of clue. Saying the four-word sentence walks you through all four, so you never leave one out.
cards.scaffoldStarter: D is for ____. E is for ____. S is for ____. A is for ____.
scaffoldSteps: Take the first letter of each.
coachPrompts: Which of the four do you spot most easily?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own sentence from D, E, S and A.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your sentence stop you forgetting one of the four?

hookFact.sourceTitle: The Words Around the Word (this lesson)

cards.target: Breaking a long word into its front, middle and end
essentialFacts: A prefix is a word part on the front, like un- meaning not.
A suffix is a word part on the end, like -ful meaning full of.
The root is the main part in the middle that carries the meaning.
cards.aiExample: Cover the ends with two fingers. Whatever is left is the root. Now take one finger off at a time. Ask what that piece did. Un-happy: cover un-, find happy, then put not back on.
cards.mapping: Covering the ends turns a long scary word into a short familiar one. Uncovering them one at a time shows what each part changed.
cards.scaffoldStarter: Cover the front: ____. Cover the end: ____. What is left is ____.
scaffoldSteps: Find a long word with a prefix or suffix.
Cover the ends and read what is left.
Say what each end did to the meaning.
coachPrompts: What does the root mean on its own, before the parts go back on?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own way to break a long word into parts.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Why is finding the root first easier than reading the whole word at once?

history.title: Which Clue Is It?

items.content: A drought, which means a long time with no rain, hit the farms.
Nocturnal animals, that is, animals awake at night, filled the woods.
She loved citrus such as lemons, limes, and oranges.
He packed utensils like a fork, a spoon, and a knife.
The room was immaculate. I had never seen it so clean.
She was weary after the hike, and I was tired too.
The street was not busy; instead it was completely deserted.
He is usually generous, but that day he was stingy.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Word Detective |
|---|---|---|---|
| Naming the clue | Guesses a type | Names the type | Names the type and quotes the words that gave it away |
| The meaning | A guess with no reason | A reasonable meaning | A meaning that fits the whole sentence when read back |
| Knowing when to stop | Keeps guessing | Says it was hard | Says there was no clue and names what to do instead |

history.title: Word Check

questions.question: "A glacier, a huge slow-moving river of ice, carved this valley." Which clue is that?
options: An example clue, since it lists some cases
A definition clue, since it says what it means
A synonym clue, since a matching word is near
An antonym clue, since a flipping word is near
questions.correctAnswer: A definition clue, since it says what it means

questions.question: "The room was not tidy; it was a shambles." What does the word not tell you?
options: A shambles means the opposite of tidy
A shambles means about the same as tidy
A shambles is a kind of room in a house
A shambles is a word nobody uses any more
questions.correctAnswer: A shambles means the opposite of tidy

questions.question: Which small words most often warn you that an opposite is coming?
options: such as, like, including
first, next, finally
but, however, instead
and, also, as well

questions.question: The word unbreakable has a prefix and a suffix. What is the root?
options: unbreak
break
breakable
able

questions.question: You read a sentence with a hard word and there is no clue anywhere. What is the smart move?
options: Keep re-reading it until a meaning appears
Skip the whole page and start a new book
Pick any meaning and carry on regardless
Ask somebody or look it up in a dictionary
questions.correctAnswer: Ask somebody or look it up in a dictionary

questions.question: "She packed produce: apples, carrots, and lettuce." What does produce mean, and how do you know?
questions.expectedAnswer: Produce means fruits and vegetables. Nobody defined it, but the list of apples, carrots and lettuce gives examples, and all three are fruits or vegetables. That is an example clue.

questions.question: Write your own sentence that gives a synonym clue for a hard word.
questions.expectedAnswer: Answers vary. A full answer uses a hard word and puts a word nearby that means nearly the same, so a reader could work the hard word out. For example: The trail was treacherous, and the guide warned us it was dangerous.

reflections.text: What is a word you worked out from a sentence this week?
Is it harder for you to spot a clue, or to admit there is not one? Why?

history.title: Word Questions Kids Ask

data.question: What if my guess is wrong? 🤔
data.answer: That happens to everyone, and it is fine. Read the sentence again with your meaning in it. If it sounds odd, your guess was off. Trying and checking is the whole method.

data.question: Is it cheating to use a dictionary?
data.answer: No. It is the right move when there is no clue. Good readers do both. They work words out when they can, and they look them up when they cannot.

data.question: Do prefixes always mean the same thing? ✂️
data.answer: Usually, but not always. Un- almost always means not. In- often means not, as in invisible, yet in include it does not. Check your guess against the sentence.

data.question: Why do books use hard words at all?
data.answer: Because some ideas need an exact word. Furious is not quite angry. Writers pick the word that fits, and then often plant a clue nearby for you.

data.question: Does this work for people's names? 📖
data.answer: Not really. A name does not have a meaning you can work out from the sentence. Sound it out, keep going, and let the story tell you who they are.

data.question: How many times do I need a word before I know it?
data.answer: More than once. Most people need to meet a word several times, in different places, before it sticks. So working it out today and forgetting it is normal, not failure.

data.title: A Clue Hunt for a Reading Buddy
data.instructions: Write four sentences, each hiding a hard word with a different kind of clue. Test them on a partner who has never seen them.
data.fitReason: Spotting a clue is easier than building one. Writing a sentence that carries a clue without giving the word away forces a student to know exactly how each clue type works.

brief.context: Your class is making a clue-hunt page for the grade below. You get four hard words from your teacher, one card per word, and one partner to test on.
brief.audience: A younger reader who does not know the four words
brief.drivingQuestion: How do you write a sentence that lets a reader work out a hard word, without simply telling them the answer?
brief.seedDirection: Use a different kind of clue for each of your four sentences. If two of yours are the same kind, swap one.
lockedLessonFacts: A definition clue tells you the meaning straight out.
An example clue shows cases instead.
A synonym clue puts a word nearby that means nearly the same.
An antonym clue puts a word nearby that means the opposite.
openQuestions: Which clue type is hardest to write, and why?
How much help is too much help?
How will you know your partner really worked it out?
stakeholders: The younger reader who will use the page
Your partner, who tests every sentence
The teacher who collects the cards
criteria: Four sentences, each using a different kind of clue
The hard word is never defined in plain words except in the definition one
A partner works out at least three of the four without help
Each card says which clue type it uses on the back
brief.deliverable: Four finished cards, plus one sentence: which clue your partner found easiest, and which one you had to rewrite.

parallelExample.context: A student had the word drenched and kept writing it means very wet.
parallelExample.move: She changed it to: He came in drenched, and a puddle grew under his coat. Her partner got it at once, and nobody had been told the meaning.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: She showed the result instead of stating the meaning, which is what an example clue does.

supports.frameStarter: My word is ____. My clue is a ____ clue. The part that gives it away is ____.
frameChoices: A matching word in the next sentence
An opposite after the word but
coachPrompts: Did your partner work it out, or did they already know the word?
Which sentence gave too much away?
Are all four of your clue types different?

data.coachHint: Four words. Four different clues. Test them.
